rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 describe a single-season (2002) split-plot field experiment at PAU Regional Station, Bathinda, India, on cotton with three drip water levels x three N rates vs check-basin, under normal and paired sowing. Q2: Section 3.1 and Table 4 report that drip with the same water and N as check-basin raised seed cotton yield from 1624 to 2144 kg/ha (32% increase, significant at LSD 0.05); drip at 75% water still gave 12% higher yield than check-basin.
rows.notes: The passage describes Ad El-wahed & Ali (2013) on maize, sprinkler vs drip, in Egypt; this cited study is a cotton trial in India comparing drip with check-basin (surface) irrigation, so the crop and comparator differ from the passage, but the technology (drip) and effect (higher yield) are tested directly. Q3: one method only (plot yield measurement). Q4: yield components (bolls/plant, branches, stick weight, seed cotton:stick ratio) were recorded, but the mechanism for the yield gain (greater dry matter allocation to bolls with optimal water availability) is attributed to Mateos et al., not measured as an intermediate variable; bolls/plant actually declined under drip. Q5: one site, one soil (loamy sand), one crop, one season. Q6: replicated plots only. Q7: yield gain was found to depend on water level (lost at 0.2 Epan) and N rate, but authors do not state these as requirements; 'suited to semi-arid areas' is from literature. Q8: no limitations stated beyond 'under these experimental conditions'. Q9: only LSD at 5%, no SD/SE/CI.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 describe a single-season field experiment on cotton comparing drip (0.4, 0.3, 0.2 Epan) with check-basin irrigation under two planting methods. Q2: Section 3.1 and Tables 4, 6, 7 report that drip at 0.3 Epan used 25% less irrigation water (41.1 vs 54.6 cm) with 12% higher yield than check-basin; drip under paired sowing used half the irrigation water (27.3 cm) with 20% higher yield; WUE rose from 17.6 to 22.1 kg/ha cm (26%) with the same water applied and to 27.3 under paired sowing; authors state beneficial effects of drip can be realized by saving 50% water or 25% water and 25% N without yield loss.
rows.notes: The passage refers to Ad El-wahed & Ali (2013) on maize with sprinkler vs drip in Egypt; this study is cotton in India with drip vs check-basin, so crop and comparator differ, but water saving and water productivity under drip are own measured results. Q3: single method (measured irrigation inputs, gravimetric profile water, plot yield). Q4: water expense components were measured (Table 6) but no intermediate variable such as percolation, soil evaporation or soil water distribution was measured; reduced percolation is asserted in the conclusions, not measured. Q5: one site/soil/crop/season. Q6: plot scale; the conclusion about bringing more area under irrigation is an extrapolation. Q7: no stated requirement for the water-saving effect from own findings. Q8: no limitations stated. Q9: no dispersion measure, only LSD at 5%.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is likely miscited for the passage (which names Ad El-wahed & Ali 2013, maize, Egypt, sprinkler vs drip); ratings were made on the technology (drip) and function fields, with the crop/comparator mismatch recorded in notes.
